title: GraphQL and Advanced API Protocols
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# GraphQL and Advanced API Protocols ##### 147 requests to render one screen A mobile team was debugging why their dashboard took eleven seconds to load on a 3G connection in a tier-2 city. The trace told the story: one request to fetch the user, one for their organization, one for each of 12 projects, then for each project one request for its issues, and for each issue one for its author. 147 round trips. Each carrying full response objects when the screen displayed four fields. The API was well-designed REST — clean resources, sensible verbs, proper status codes. It was simply the wrong shape for the question being asked. This is the **N+1 problem**, and it is the reason Facebook built GraphQL in 2012. Understanding when a different protocol is the right answer — and being able to defend the choice — is a genuinely intermediate skill, because it requires knowing the trade-offs rather than the marketing. ##### Over-fetching and under-fetching Two specific inefficiencies REST makes hard to avoid. **Over-fetching** — the endpoint returns more than you need. `GET /users/4471` returns 40 fields including a bio, avatar variants and preferences when your UI shows a name and email. Wasted bandwidth, wasted parsing, and a coupling problem: the endpoint's shape is a compromise across all its consumers. **Under-fetching** — the endpoint returns less than you need, forcing follow-up calls. You have the user, now you need their organization, then that organization's plan. Each hop is a full round trip, and on high-latency connections round trips dominate everything else. REST's usual mitigations — `?fields=name,email` sparse fieldsets, `?include=organization` compound documents, or purpose-built `/dashboard-summary` endpoints — work, but each is a bespoke convention the server must implement and the client must learn. GraphQL's contribution is to make "ask for exactly this shape" the default protocol behaviour rather than an extension. ##### Queries, mutations, and variables A GraphQL API exposes **one endpoint** (`POST /graphql`) and a **schema** describing every type and field available. The client sends a query describing the shape it wants; the response mirrors that shape exactly. ```graphql query RepoIssues($owner: String!, $name: String!, $first: Int = 20, $after: String) { repository(owner: $owner, name: $name) { name stargazerCount issues(first: $first, after: $after, states: OPEN, orderBy: {field: CREATED_AT, direction: DESC}) { totalCount pageInfo { hasNextPage endCursor } nodes { number title createdAt author { login ... on User { name company } } labels(first: 5) { nodes { name color } } comments { totalCount } } } } } ``` That single request replaces the 147. Note the pieces an intermediate practitioner should recognize: - **Named operation** (`RepoIssues`) — required for good server-side logging and essential for persisted queries. - **Variables** with types (`$owner: String!` — the `!` means non-null) and defaults. **Always use variables rather than string interpolation**; it is the GraphQL equivalent of parameterized SQL and prevents both injection and query-cache misses. - **Arguments on fields** (`states: OPEN`, `orderBy:`) — filtering happens at the field level. - **Inline fragments** (`... on User`) for interface and union types, where `author` might be a `User` or a `Bot`. **Mutations** are the write half, structurally identical but conventionally taking a single `input` object and returning the mutated entity plus errors: ```graphql mutation AddComment($input: AddCommentInput!) { addComment(input: $input) { commentEdge { node { id url createdAt } } } } ``` with variables `{"input": {"subjectId": "I_kwDO...", "body": "Confirmed on 2.4.1"}}`. Two behaviours that surprise REST practitioners: **GraphQL returns HTTP 200 even for errors**, with problems listed in a top-level `errors` array; and responses can be **partially successful** — `data` populated for the fields that resolved, `errors` describing those that did not. Your client must check `errors` on every response, not just the status code. ```python import os, requests QUERY = """ query RepoIssues($owner: String!, $name: String!, $after: String) { repository(owner: $owner, name: $name) { issues(first: 50, after: $after, states: OPEN) { pageInfo { hasNextPage endCursor } nodes { number title author { login } } } } rateLimit { cost remaining resetAt } } """ def fetch_all_issues(owner: str, name: str): session = requests.Session() session.headers.update({ "Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['GITHUB_TOKEN']}", "Content-Type": "application/json", }) cursor, out = None, [] while True: r = session.post( "https://api.github.com/graphql", json={"query": QUERY, "variables": {"owner": owner, "name": name, "after": cursor}}, timeout=30, ) r.raise_for_status() body = r.json() if "errors" in body: # HTTP 200 can still be a failure raise RuntimeError(body["errors"]) issues = body["data"]["repository"]["issues"] out.extend(issues["nodes"]) limit = body["data"]["rateLimit"] print(f"cost={limit['cost']} remaining={limit['remaining']}") if not issues["pageInfo"]["hasNextPage"]: return out cursor = issues["pageInfo"]["endCursor"] ``` ##### Pagination and rate limits in GraphQL GraphQL standardized cursor pagination through the **Relay connection specification**, and once you recognize the shape you will see it everywhere: ```text issues(first: 50, after: "Y3Vyc29yOjUw") { totalCount pageInfo { hasNextPage hasPreviousPage startCursor endCursor } edges { cursor node { ... } } # edges carry relationship metadata nodes { ... } # shortcut when you don't need edge data } ``` `first`/`after` page forward, `last`/`before` page backward. Loop on `pageInfo.hasNextPage`, passing `endCursor`. The `edges` layer exists because the *relationship* can have attributes (a `role` on a membership edge, for instance) distinct from the node itself. **Rate limiting works differently**, and this catches people out. Because one GraphQL request can be arbitrarily expensive, providers do not count requests — they compute a **cost** per query. GitHub allocates 5,000 points per hour, calculated from the number of nodes a query could return. A query asking for 100 repositories × 100 issues each is charged for the potential 10,000 nodes, whether or not they exist. Servers also defend themselves with **query depth limits**, **complexity analysis**, **query allowlists** and **persisted queries** (the client sends a hash instead of the query text). As a consumer this means: request the smallest `first:` value that meets your need, avoid deeply nested speculative fields, and read the `rateLimit` field the API exposes. ##### Protocol comparison | | REST | GraphQL | gRPC | SOAP | |---|---|---|---|---| | **Transport/format** | HTTP + JSON | HTTP + JSON | HTTP/2 + Protobuf | HTTP + XML | | **Shape control** | Server-defined | Client-defined | Server-defined (schema) | Server-defined (WSDL) | | **Schema/typing** | Optional (OpenAPI) | Mandatory, introspectable | Mandatory (`.proto`) | Mandatory (XSD) | | **Performance** | Good | Good; fewer round trips | Excellent — binary, multiplexed | Poor — verbose XML | | **Streaming** | SSE / chunked | Subscriptions | First-class bidirectional | No | | **Caching** | Excellent (HTTP caching) | Hard (single POST endpoint) | Manual | Poor | | **Browser support** | Native | Native | Needs gRPC-Web proxy | Native | | **Tooling maturity** | Universal | Strong | Strong in backend ecosystems | Legacy, enterprise | Where each genuinely wins: **REST** — public APIs with diverse unknown consumers, anything benefiting from HTTP caching and CDNs, simple CRUD, and situations where the lowest possible integration friction matters. Still the correct default for most public APIs. **GraphQL** — clients with varied and evolving data needs (mobile apps, dashboards), deeply related data where N+1 hurts, and organizations wanting one API surface over many backend services. GitHub, Shopify and Contentful all offer it alongside REST for exactly these reasons. **gRPC** — internal service-to-service communication where latency and throughput dominate: binary Protobuf encoding, HTTP/2 multiplexing, strict contracts and generated clients in every language. Not browser-native without a proxy, so rarely a public-facing choice. Empirical work on GraphQL migrations (Brito et al., 2019) found meaningful reductions in returned data size and query complexity, but also real learning-curve and tooling costs — the trade-off is genuine in both directions. **SOAP** — you do not choose it; you inherit it. Banking, insurance, telecom, government and legacy ERP systems still expose it. Know that it means XML envelopes, a WSDL contract, and often WS-Security headers. ##### Streaming and long-polling For data that arrives continuously rather than on request: **Long polling** — the client requests, the server holds the connection open until data exists or a timeout fires, then the client immediately re-requests. Works everywhere, no special infrastructure, but ties up a connection and adds latency at each cycle. **Server-Sent Events (SSE)** — a single long-lived HTTP response streaming `text/event-stream` chunks. Unidirectional (server → client), auto-reconnecting, trivially proxied. This is what LLM APIs use for token streaming, and it is usually the right choice for one-way feeds. **WebSockets** — full-duplex over a persistent connection. Use when the client must also push frequently: collaborative editing, chat, live trading. **GraphQL subscriptions** — typically WebSocket-based, letting a client subscribe to a typed event stream defined in the schema. **Webhooks** — the server calls you. Best for infrequent, high-value events where holding a connection would be wasteful, which describes most business integrations. ```mermaid flowchart TD A[Need data from a service] --> B{Continuous stream
or discrete request?} B -->|discrete| C{Client needs vary
widely / deeply nested?} C -->|yes| D[GraphQL] C -->|no| E{Internal service-to-service,
latency critical?} E -->|yes| F[gRPC] E -->|no| G[REST] B -->|continuous| H{Direction?} H -->|server to client only| I[SSE] H -->|bidirectional| J[WebSocket] H -->|infrequent events| K[Webhook] ``` ##### Common pitfalls - **String-interpolating variables** into the query text instead of using `variables`. - **Only checking the HTTP status** and missing the `errors` array on a 200. - **Requesting `first: 100` reflexively**, inflating cost and risking timeouts. - **Ignoring the `rateLimit` field** that most GraphQL APIs helpfully expose. - **Assuming client-side N+1 is solved** — it moves to the server, where DataLoader-style batching is needed; a badly implemented resolver is still N+1. - **Treating GraphQL as strictly better than REST.** You lose HTTP caching, gain query-cost complexity, and add client tooling. - **Not handling partial data** — `data` can be populated while `errors` is non-empty. - **Forgetting inline fragments** on union/interface fields, producing empty objects. ##### Your hands-on tie-in The practical task: using a public GraphQL API — GitHub's is the richest, `countries.trevorblades.com` needs no auth — write **queries with variables that fetch nested related data in one request**, and handle **cursor-based pagination**. Then do the instructive comparison: count how many REST calls the same result would require. That number is the argument for GraphQL, in your own data. The mini project: build an integration pulling **related data in efficient single-round-trip queries** — a repository, its issues, and their authors — with **connection-based pagination**, storing the **normalized** results in a database. Normalization is the interesting constraint: GraphQL returns a nested tree, your database wants flat related tables, so you will write a shredding step that splits the tree into `repos`, `issues` and `authors` rows with foreign keys. Log the `rateLimit.cost` per page and tune `first:` to see the cost model respond. For the assignment, explain **over-fetching and under-fetching** and how GraphQL addresses them, then compare **REST, GraphQL and gRPC** with one scenario where each is best. Argue from constraints — consumer diversity, round-trip cost, caching needs, browser reachability — rather than from preference, and mention what GraphQL gives up (HTTP caching, simplicity, predictable server cost) to earn what it provides. ##### Key takeaways - Over-fetching wastes payload and under-fetching multiplies round trips; GraphQL makes client-specified response shape the protocol default. - Always use typed variables, name your operations, and check the `errors` array — GraphQL returns HTTP 200 for failures and supports partial success. - Relay connections (`first`/`after`, `pageInfo`, `edges`/`nodes`) are the standard pagination shape; GraphQL rate limits are cost-based, so request the smallest page that works. - REST for public, cacheable, diverse-consumer APIs; GraphQL for varied client needs and deeply related data; gRPC for internal low-latency service calls; SOAP is inherited, not chosen. - For continuous data, match the mechanism to direction and frequency: SSE for server-to-client streams, WebSockets for bidirectional, webhooks for infrequent business events.
